one_liner: DeepMind's archived decorator-driven JIT library for CPython 3.7; first-party 7-9.5x on Richards, 5x slower on unpack_sequence.
what_it_does: S6 is a CPython extension (built with CMake and pybind11) that JIT-compiles Python functions without patching CPython's source: you import s6 and wrap an entry function with @s6.jit, and while that call runs S6 swaps the interpreter's frame-evaluation hook so the function and everything it calls go through S6's own interpreter and, once hot, compiled code. s6.inspect(fn) exposes the strongjit IR, is_compiled, force_compile, deoptimize and an IR evaluator for debugging. It only supports CPython 3.7 built with frame pointers and is meant to be built inside the project's Docker image.
how_it_is_fast: S6's ceval-like interpreter collects type feedback, and an Oracle counts executed bytecodes to pick hot code objects for asynchronous compilation. Bytecode is translated to strongjit, an SSA IR with block arguments; optimisation passes run on it, functions are specialised on the type of their first argument behind guards with deoptimisation back to CPython frames, and boxed int/float/bool arithmetic is unboxed. Attribute and global loads use V8-style hidden classes (class IDs hidden in the top 20 bits of a dict's ma_version_tag or a type's tp_flags) so they become guarded fixed-slot loads, and attributes that never change are treated as constants; the IR is lowered to x86-64 machine code with asmjit.
when_to_use: Studying how to build a V8-style JIT (hidden classes, SSA IR, deoptimisation) as a CPython library: the README is a detailed design write-up and the C++ source is Apache-2.0.

Object-oriented pure-Python hot loops (method calls, attribute access) on a CPython 3.7 you control: Richards is the case with the first-party 7x (100 iterations) and 9.5x (internal machines) figures.
Pure-Python floating-point code such as the raytrace benchmark (3-4.5x first-party), where unboxing applies.
x86-64 Linux setups that can rebuild CPython 3.7 with -fno-omit-frame-pointer and run the Docker build.
when_not_to_use: Anything needing support or a current Python: the repository was archived on 2023-07-05 with a single import commit, DeepMind stopped work on it, and only CPython 3.7 is supported.
Code dominated by C-API calls such as NumPy: the README says these are bottlenecked by C API call time.

Large functions or heavy tuple/list unpacking: unpack_sequence ran 5x slower (0.2x) because the hot loop stays in S6's own interpreter, which is slower than ceval.c; the README advises splitting big functions.

Stock distribution CPython builds: without frame pointers JIT compilation 'might crash', and the --wrap=PyFrame_FastToLocalsWithError link step is not in the release, so compilation 'might misbehave'; pyperf segfaults under S6 (benchmark docstrings).
Non-x86-64 hosts: code generation targets x86 only.

integration.form: Python C++ extension module (pybind11) built from source with CMake/Ninja; Docker image recommended
integration.dependencies: CPython 3.7 shared library, abseil-cpp, asmjit, pybind11, pybind11_abseil, re2, udis86, cppitertools, googletest (pinned via FetchContent in src/CMake/deps.cmake), protobuf from the system
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, clang (Dockerfile uses clang 13), CMake 3.16.3+, CPython 3.7 configured with --enable-shared and built with -fno-omit-frame-pointer
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux (Ubuntu 20.04 Docker image); no other targets
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the design relies on the GIL (type modifications 'stop the world', which the README calls easy because of the GIL), and compilation runs asynchronously from the Oracle
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: no CPython source changes and only a @s6.jit decorator on the entry point, but it needs a frame-pointer CPython 3.7 build plus S6's own build, and some workloads run slower

gotchas: Harness flaw: @s6.jit is applied at import time (in the Richards class body and on module-level functions), and the decorator calls Initialize(adopt_types=true), which adopts all existing types, swaps the generic tp_setattro of every adoptable type for S6's GenericSetAttrUsingClasses (string interning plus a class attribute-map lookup) and hooks PyType_Type.tp_new. The 'Default Python 3.7' baseline in richards.py, raytrace.py and the unpack_sequence scripts is therefore timed on a CPython already instrumented by S6, not stock CPython; Richards' attribute-store-heavy loop pays the wrapper, which can inflate the reported speedup by an unmeasured amount.

Each script times one wall-clock run per mode (time.time() or perf_counter), baseline first and S6 second in the same process, with no repetitions; richards.py discards _run's correctness result (holdCount 9297 / qpktCount 23246), so a wrong result would still print a speedup, and its default is 50 iterations while the README quotes 100. The S6 time includes JIT warm-up and compilation.

Specialisation is on the first argument's type only; hidden classes are not used for objects with custom __getattr__/__setattr__ or a negative tp_dictoffset, and any dict change made outside S6 resets the class ID to 0, dropping that object off the fast path.
The public numbers come from 'internal dev machines' with no CPU or build named; the Docker baseline CPython is the unpinned 3.7 branch built without PGO and with frame pointers kept.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick S6 only as a design reference: for running code, Cinder's CinderX extension (actively released for CPython 3.14, 1.5-3.8x over its own interpreter) or CPython's built-in copy-and-patch JIT (about 7-8% geomean, supported) are the practical CPython JITs, and Numba or Hana Jit fit numeric kernels better.
verified_claims_summary: First-party only: the README reports Richards about 7x over 'the default Python 3.7 interpreter' at 100 iterations 'depending on your hardware' and 9.5x on unnamed internal dev machines, raytrace 3-4.5x, and unpack_sequence 0.2x (slow variant) or 0.97x (fast variant). The numbers come from single-run scripts in src/benchmarks that time the baseline and then the S6 run in the same process; the public build is clang 13 against a non-PGO, frame-pointer CPython 3.7, and no independent reproduction was found.
status_note: Abandoned: archived 2023-07-05 after one Copybara import commit (2022-09-14) and tied to CPython 3.7; Apache-2.0 (src/LICENSE and per-file headers), so the code can be copied, but in practice it is a reference design rather than a usable dependency.
